brief.situation: You are the vulnerability analyst at Tamsin Mutual, a fictional insurer. At 08:00 the weekly scan lands with four findings rated high or critical, and the threat feed reports that one of them was added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog this morning. There is staff for one emergency change. Prioritize, reduce the exposure, check for compromise, validate and report.
handover: Every scan score here is fictional. The VPN gateway carries every remote session; the backup gateway can carry about a third of them.
Saturday's maintenance window is the normal route for patches.
howItWorks: Each task takes analyst time: choose it, then let the work finish, which moves the clock by the minutes that task takes. The attacker keeps working on the same clock.
New alerts and log lines appear in the console as they happen.
When you declare the incident contained, you notify, write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: how you ranked the four findings, what you did about the top one and in what order, and how you know it is fixed.

parts.label: Prioritization
parts.criteria: Ranks the internet-facing VPN flaw first because it is actively exploited (KEV) with a high EPSS, despite a lower CVSS; places the internal HR flaw in the window, accepts or schedules the isolated lab box, and treats the banner-only MAIL01 match as a false positive only after checking the backport.
parts.modelAnswer: CVSS rates severity, not likelihood. The VPN flaw is in KEV, internet-facing and on our most important remote-access asset, so it was the emergency; HR-APP01 is internal with no known exploitation, LAB-07 is isolated, and MAIL01's fix was backported.

parts.label: Mitigation
parts.criteria: Applies the vendor workaround (a compensating control) at once and then patches, rather than waiting for the window; or takes the gateway offline if needed.
parts.modelAnswer: I turned the portal off with the vendor's workaround within minutes, then ran the emergency upgrade.

parts.label: Verification
parts.criteria: Checks the gateway for prior exploitation (patching does not remove a web shell) and rescans after the patch to validate.
parts.modelAnswer: Because it was exploited in the wild before we knew, I ran the integrity check for a web shell, and rescanned after the upgrade to confirm the fixed version.

expertPath.text: Enrich all four: the VPN flaw is in KEV, internet-facing, EPSS 0.94. Escalate and apply the vendor workaround.
Run the emergency upgrade on the gateway.
Check the gateway for a web shell, rescan to validate, check MAIL01's backport, and schedule or accept the rest.
Tell IT leadership, the change board and the VPN owner; record the VPN as the top risk and MAIL01 as a false positive.

fixed.headline: Good: risk, not raw scores
fixed.body: The finding with the lowest CVSS of the four was the only one being exploited. You closed it first, checked for compromise and proved the fix.

fixedLate.headline: Fixed, with gaps
fixedLate.body: The gateway is safe now. The criteria show what cost you: a late fix, a missed check for compromise, or no validation.

breached.headline: Exploited before it was closed
breached.body: Spending the emergency change on the highest CVSS left the exploited, internet-facing flaw open. KEV and exposure come first.

stillExposed.headline: Closed while exposed
stillExposed.body: A KEV flaw on an internet-facing gateway does not wait for Saturday, and a patch does not remove a web shell already planted.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Prioritize by exploitation, exposure and asset value: the VPN gateway flaw is in KEV, has a high EPSS and faces the internet, so it outranks the higher CVSS scores on an internal server and an isolated lab box. Escalate, apply the vendor workaround at once, run the emergency upgrade, check the gateway for a web shell, rescan to validate, confirm the MAIL01 banner match is a backported false positive, and schedule or formally accept the rest.
